Operations Centers

A Security Operations Center (SOC) is a centralized team that monitors, detects, and responds

to cyber threats in real time, and it is a critical element of incident management. Without

effective response.

Box 11 Case studies: Voluntary cyber resilience centers (CRCs)

Los Angeles Cyber Resilience Center

The Port of Los Angeles launched its Cyber Resilience Center in January 2022 to serve

as a “system of systems” for rapid sharing of cyber threat indicators and collective

defense among terminal operators, shipping lines, rail, trucking, and other supply-chain

stakeholders. Building on the Port’s internal Cyber Security Operations Center (established

in 2014), the CRC centralizes and automates the exchange of cyber indicators and defensive

measures, offers training and tabletop exercises, and provides an early warning function

to protect cargo flow. The port’s board approved an agreement with IBM in late 2020 to

design, operate, and maintain the CRC, leveraging threat intelligence and orchestration

technologies.

What Does This Report Do?

This report draws on a global survey of 109 port stakeholders, in-depth interviews, and desk-based

regulatory mapping. The outcome is a unique overview of the current cybersecurity landscape in the

port sector and a series of actionable recommendations, with a particular focus on ports in low- and

middle-income countries. The findings and recommendations are split into three themes:

1. Policy 2. Practice 3. Barriers

resourcing, and consistent practice are still far from the

are often even more acute: policy coverage is thinner, skills

gaps are wider, and resources are more constrained. As

Box 8 Case studies: Delivery and communication styles of cybersecurity

training methods

The Port of Antwerp-Bruges demonstrated the importance of training delivery methods

by using creative approaches, including organizing a Cybersecurity Escape Room and

cybersecurity-focused shows. While these initiatives require significant effort, lower-intensity

measures can also be highly effective. For example, inviting a speaker from a company that has

experienced a cyber incident has proven successful in raising employee awareness.

Maintaining continuous awareness requires ongoing communication, not just periodic

training events. The Gambia Ports Authority, for instance, sends weekly warning emails to

staff highlighting social engineering threats such as phishing, helping to keep security

top-of-mind throughout the year.

Economic barriers arise when different parties do not share the same goals and problems spill over:

if one operator cuts back on cybersecurity, it can raise risks for everyone else, creating so-called

negative externalities. Some parties may be tempted to benefit from others’ investments without

contributing themselves, free-riding8 on others (Moore 2010). On top of that, information gaps make

it hard to assess risks clearly and learn from past events. This chapter examines these key barriers

to improving cybersecurity in ports and first discusses human capacity barriers (3.1), then financial

barriers (3.2), and finally economic barriers (3.3).

2.1 Evaluating Risk: Knowing What You Are Up Against

2.1.1 How Do Incidents Occur?

Understanding how incidents enter port systems is a prerequisite for protecting them. The

overwhelming majority of port cyber incidents documented in the literature involve the exploitation

of well-known, preventable weaknesses rather than novel techniques (Meland et al. 2021; Chubb et

al. 2022; Badea et al. 2025). This has important implications: for most ports, basic and consistent

implementation of established protective controls would materially reduce exposure of information

and operational technologies (IT and OT).

Synthesizing incident data and threat analysis from various sources, the evidence consistently

points to several recurring entry points in port environments:

• phishing and social engineering targeting staff,

• exploitation of unpatched software vulnerabilities in IT systems,

Why Does This Report Matter?

Ports play a critical role in international trade, regional and domestic economic activities, and the

well-being of people and societies. Today, ports are no longer simply physical infrastructure; they

have become digital systems. Port authorities, terminal operators, shipping lines, logistics providers,

and customs are increasingly linked through shared digital platforms. This improves efficiency and

transparency in ports, but it also means that a breach in one part of the ecosystem can cascade

across others. Cybersecurity in ports is therefore a collective responsibility, and the entire ecosystem

is only as strong as its weakest link.

Box 7 Case studies: Improving port resilience through business

continuity planning

The Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) conducts regular cybersecurity

tabletop exercises with key partners. The one conducted in April 2024 brought together

40 international participants from the maritime sector. The exercise simulated

simultaneous cyberattacks across ports in multiple regions, deliberately testing the

coordination mechanisms between port authorities operating under different national

regulatory frameworks. The inclusion of international ports reflects a deliberate design

choice: because digital supply chain cyber incidents rarely respect national boundaries,

response capacity needs to be practiced across borders, not just within them.

results.text:
on 8 June 2023 by the Dirección General del Territorio Marítimo y de Marina Mercante

(DIRECTEMAR). The circular establishes mandatory cybersecurity and information-security

requirements for port facilities as part of maritime cyber risk management. It requires

ports to implement a structured cyber risk management system aligned with international

standards and to integrate this system into security assessments and port protection

plans under the ISPS Code. Ports must identify and mitigate cyber risks affecting critical

systems—such as access control, communications, cargo handling systems, and other

operational technologies—designate a responsible cybersecurity officer, and report

cyber incidents to the competent maritime authority. Compliance is verified through a

combination of internal and external audits, and strategically significant port

facilities are required to incorporate cyber risk management into their overall

security studies and general security plans.

2.2.3 Operationalizing Incident Response Using Security

Operations Centers

A Security Operations Center (SOC) is a centralized team that monitors, detects, and responds

to cyber threats in real time, and it is a critical element of incident management. Without

one, organizations may struggle to identify escalation channels, delaying or preventing

effective response.

Survey findings revealed an unexpected pattern. Middle-income countries were least likely to

operate an in-house or managed SOC, while high-income and low-income countries showed the

highest rates of SOC outsourcing. Yet interviews suggest an encouraging shift, with more low- and

middle-income port operators turning to third-party SOC services as a pragmatic way to build

capability where in-house expertise is limited. Clear reporting protocols across all staff are equally

2.1 Evaluating Risk: Knowing What You Are Up Against

2.1.1 How Do Incidents Occur?

Understanding how incidents enter port systems is a prerequisite for protecting them. The

overwhelming majority of port cyber incidents documented in the literature involve the exploitation

of well-known, preventable weaknesses rather than novel techniques (Meland et al. 2021; Chubb et

al. 2022; Badea et al. 2025). This has important implications: for most ports, basic and consistent

implementation of established protective controls would materially reduce exposure of information

and operational technologies (IT and OT).

Limitations

The findings are subject to several limitations common to survey-based research. First, the analysis

relies on self-reported data, which may be subject to social desirability bias, including the potential

overstatement of cybersecurity maturity or underreporting of incidents and vulnerabilities. Second,

the number of responses limits the extent to which findings can be considered representative of the

global port sector. Third, although the survey was available in three languages, some organizations

may not have been reached equally, particularly in regions where English, French, or Spanish are

less commonly used in professional settings. Accordingly, the results should be viewed as indicative
